content: Disagreements during the analysis process were resolved by consulting a third member of the research team to discuss the inclusion of studies. Data were extracted using a pre-tested form that captured patient characteristics (including subgroups identified by the Guideline Development Group, or GDG), diagnosis, treatment details (such as dosage and schedule), clinical setting, follow-up, and outcomes. Two investigators independently abstracted the data. For statistical analysis, risk ratios and odds ratios were calculated by pooling results from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies using a random-effects model. Moderate to high heterogeneity (I² > 50%) was explored. Relative effects were converted into absolute effects using a representative baseline risk agreed upon by the GDG. When non-randomized studies with a single group were included, pooled event proportions and confidence intervals were calculated using the generic inverse variance method. For continuous outcomes, mean differences or standardized mean differences (when different scales were used) were calculated. Forest plots of meta-analyses were provided to the GDG when possible. Studies on patient values, preferences, acceptability, equity, and feasibility were identified through two methods. First, relevant studies were flagged during the screening of treatment effects and cost studies by two investigators. Second, a separate search was conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO from January 2000 to July 2015, using keywords related to sexually transmitted infections (STIs) combined with terms such as preference, adherence, satisfaction, attitudes, health utilities, value, equity, and feasibility. This search yielded 2,563 unique references, of which 162 studies were retrieved for full-text review. Any study design addressing equity or feasibility was included. Adherence data from RCTs or non-randomized studies were synthesized and presented in evidence profiles for each PICO question. Patient utility and health status value studies examined how patients valued alternative health states and their treatment experiences. Non-utility studies quantitatively assessed patient views, attitudes, satisfaction, or preferences using questionnaires or scales. Qualitative studies explored patient perspectives on treatment options through methods such as focus groups and interviews. Seventeen studies were included, many of which informed evidence specific to gonorrhea. Resource use and cost data were obtained from the literature, focusing on the direct costs of medications. Costs were calculated based on treatment regimens identified by the GDG, including dosage, duration, and procurement costs (with a 25% markup for procurement). The final cost per treatment course was determined by multiplying the number of doses per day by the treatment duration and adding 25% of the procurement cost. Unit prices were sourced from the 2014 MSH/WHO International Drug Price Indicator Guide and other reliable sources. Major medical databases were searched for economic evaluations and technology assessments from January 2005 to July 2015. Six studies addressed the cost-effectiveness of gonorrhea treatment strategies, but no studies were found on resource use specific to gonococcal infections. The quality of evidence for treatment interventions was assessed using the GRADE approach, which evaluates study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, effect size, dose-response relationships, and other factors. Two investigators independently applied the GRADE criteria to assess the certainty of evidence. Evidence profiles for each recommendation, including critical outcomes, relative and absolute effects, and evidence quality, were made available in Web Annex D. In October 2015, the GDG convened to finalize recommendations. The meeting was co-chaired by experts in GRADE methodology and clinical management of gonorrhea. Methodologists presented evidence profiles and decision frameworks, and the GDG discussed each GRADE criterion to determine the preferred intervention. Final decisions and recommendations were developed through consensus, facilitated by the chairpersons. Disagreements were documented in the decision framework, but no disagreements arose for the final recommendations, so voting was unnecessary. Recommendations were categorized as strong or conditional, with special circumstances noted in the remarks. Research implications were also identified and presented based on evidence gaps. Following the meeting, recommendations were finalized via teleconference and electronically approved by GDG members. All decisions and discussions are documented in the evidence-to-decision frameworks in Web Annex D.
